# Education in Norway
Education in Norway has a long history dating back to around 2000 B.C., evolving through cathedral schools established in the Middle Ages to the modern folkeskole, later replaced by the grunnskole system. Compulsory education currently covers elementary (barneskole, ages 6–12) and lower secondary (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16) schooling, collectively called grunnskole. Upper secondary school (videregående skole, ages 16–19) follows and is not compulsory. The education system includes free public schools and a limited number of private schools under the Independent Schools Act of 2003, which must follow approved curricula and are government-aided.
In primary school, children focus on foundational skills without official grades, moving to graded evaluations in lower secondary school, where elective languages and practical subjects become available. Upper secondary education offers general and vocational tracks, with reforms like the 1994 “Reform 94” and the 2006 Kunnskapsløftet aiming for greater flexibility and integration between study paths. Vocational studies often combine school training with apprenticeships. Higher education comprises universities, university colleges, and private institutions, requiring a general university admissions certificate for entry. Norway’s qualifications agency, NOKUT, oversees accreditation, and grading systems have transitioned alongside the Bologna Process. Special education is integrated into local schools with support services for students with additional needs. The academic year runs from August to June with multiple breaks, and national holidays are observed throughout.
